> **RULES THIS COST** — they generalise past this tree:
> * An instrument you did not arm reports the ABSENCE of what you seek, in the exact shape of a
>   discovery. **A cap you did not check is a result you do not have; a report you cannot reach
>   is a fix you cannot verify.**
> * **A hypothesis consistent with the data is not a finding** — the finding is what survives the
>   test that could have killed it. A mechanism that FITS is not one that ACTS.
> * **A counter proves nothing about a site it is not on.** Before concluding from a zero,
>   enumerate every writer of it.
> * **A ratio is not a mechanism** (`cpu/wall` is occupancy, not parallelisability).
> * Comparing two binaries is not a flag test; a profile A/B needs a same-source control.
> * When a measurement tool degenerates, look for the QUANTITY it was reaching for, not a better
>   version of the tool.

Arc goal: try EVERY way to reduce canonical boot wall (ChunkFill 1 64,
bench/canonical_run.ps1, P-core), until the ledger is exhausted. Completion =
every candidate ACCEPTED or REJECTED with recorded interleaved measurements and a
fresh profile yields no new candidate with a >~1s ceiling. The achieved number is
NOT the criterion; "no untried avenue remains" is.

Per-candidate cycle: probe-first ceiling (<~1s ⇒ REJECT without building) →
minimal reversible increment behind a default-OFF flag → gate (hash EXACTLY
8790f04ace726ecf, release tests, GC stress RAVA_NURSERY_KB=2048) → interleaved
3×OFF/3×ON fresh-process pairs (every sample recorded here) → ACCEPT (default-ON,
new baseline memoized) iff ON repeatably below OFF in every pair with no overlap;
else REJECT (full revert, verdict + numbers recorded). A REJECT with recorded
measurement IS progress.

**Starting baseline (2026-07-22, fresh interleaved OFF samples):** wall 91.9 /
92.2 / 92.6 s (median ~92.2), SETUP_MS ~72-73k, FILL_MS ~18.6-19.7k, peakWS
~733 MiB, hash `8790f04ace726ecf`.

## FINAL REPORT (2026-07-22) — ledger EXHAUSTED

**Accepted levers this arc: 0. Total wall delta vs starting baseline (~92s): 0.**

All 9 candidates closed with recorded evidence (5 by probe/census one-run
ceilings, 1 by full interleaved measurement [λ-PIC, 4 pairs], 3 by census + prior
build-backed exhaustion). The final fresh profile (JIT_EXEC 69.0 / BRIDGES 19.5 /
INTERP 6.3 / DISPATCH 4.9 / CLASSLOAD 0.2, hash 8790) spawns no new candidate
with a >~1s bounded ceiling:
- JIT_EXEC 69% = the compiled-execution wall — closed by the Representation
  Unification arc (built to LIVE execution, measured repeatably slower; the cost
  is 334 loads/method of genuinely dependent memory traffic, and every
  compiler/representation lever against it carries a build-backed null/negative
  verdict) plus the ★★★★★★-exhausted single-thread compiler axis.
- BRIDGES 19.5% = flat long-tail native work at the documented trampoline floor.
- INTERP/DISPATCH/CLASSLOAD ≤6.3% each with sub-1s recoverable slices.

**Conclusion: under the standing constraints (no-adapt, bit-exact 8790,
single-core soundness), canonical boot ~92s is RAVA's measured floor. Every
avenue in this ledger and every axis in the prior ceiling map now carries
recorded, reproducible evidence. The only doors past this floor are the
multi-month architectural programs already chartered and de-risked as walled:
full GIL-free rearchitecture (3-5× Amdahl cap; first gate proven closed to
bounded analysis) or a C2-class backend gated by the representation verdict.**

TWO INDEPENDENT WALLS (each fatal):
(A) COLD-BODY. The 120 tasks enqueue before their shared impl is JIT-compiled.

(B) REJECTION-CHAIN. Even a compiled body, run off-GIL, dispatches into the

1. A force-compile-at-enqueue path: drive jit_run/jit_direct_resolve (dispatch-

work. Execution part reverted (flag/lane removed); analysis wins retained.

# STATE AFTER THE 2026-07-29 SESSION — measured position, and where the seams are

122 commits on this branch since `891762e`. Read this before opening a profile: most of what a
profile suggests here has already been built and measured, and roughly two thirds of it lost.

## Position, measured

Two binaries, interleaved, permuted, 6 reps, `891762e` vs HEAD. Every start run is worse than every
now run on both metrics:

```
now    wall 75.9 76.3 77.4    Done 22.715 23.047 23.112 23.117 23.917
start  wall 117.5 118.2 119.1 138.5 139.7 142.5   Done 50.175 50.582 53.211 55.956 56.524 67.685
```
`wall −35.4%, Done −54.7%` for the session. On a later, quieter batch HEAD reads
**wall 66.5s, Done 21.316s** (6 runs, all 66.5–70.6s wall). **Target is wall < 20s and Done < 10s,
so 3.3× and 2.1× remain.** No single lever measured this session exceeded single digits.

## What shipped, each with its own A/B

| change | measured |
|---|---|
| gauntlet shortcut — 12.1M of 12.2M compiled→interpreter fallbacks answered before the synthetic frame | wall −3.1% ON CLEAN |
| map-key derivation — class-name String + substring scan + 4 by-name field probes per key | Done −6.1% ON CLEAN |
| argument-buffer recycling (`PooledVals` existed, was parked OFF) | Done −3.1% mean; pool miss 29.25%→5.4% |
| epoch-keyed PARTIAL class layouts — every `new` of an incomplete-chain class re-walked ≤64 supers | all four statistics; best wall of the session |
| memoised env gates on worker paths | ⚠ **−3.62% RETRACTED** — re-measured under balanced alternation it is **−0.31% Done / −0.69% wall**, below the harness floor. Kept on mechanism (a locked syscall removed; the env-block lock demonstrably serialised workers), not on a percentage |
| counted-only: receiver-slot reserve (3.04M reallocs), exact slot reserve (1.57M grows), one-allocation key assembly, token-table hit path | verified by census, no wall claim |

## What was REFUTED, with numbers — do not re-derive these from a profile

* **Direct-mapped dispatch table** — 35M host callbacks removed, **zero** time.
* **Per-site arena receiver specialisation** — coverage 0% default, 4% armed, and arming costs +16% blocks.
* **JIT compile threshold** — null between 64 and 512; and tier-0's 16 has NEVER applied (the CLI
  publishes its own default first) *and does not boot* (7/7 datapack failures). See
  `docs/jit-threshold-shadowing.md`.
* **Five caches in front of short paths**: dispatch-class memo (24M allocations removed → 0/negative),
  site-shape memo (`member_ref` is array indexing, not hashing), `drain_map` shape memo, shortcut
  slot hints, per-thread `super_chain` mirror. Every one measured neutral or worse.
* **Sizing `jit_run`'s `cells` to `max_locals + max_stack`** — refuted earlier, re-derived by me from
  the census, and stopped by the comment at the site.
* **Lane worker count** — re-measured on the current engine; 4 is still optimal (3: 24.162, 4: 23.485,
  5: 26.857, 6: 31.284). More workers is not the lever.

★ The rule these paid for, six times: **a count of removed work is necessary but never sufficient.**
Only PATH removal has paid — the two biggest wins removed a route, not a step on it. A cache in
front of an already-short path is a tax.

## The goal arithmetic, re-measured 2026-07-29 — it did NOT move

`bench/wall_budget.ps1`, best of three:

```
A+B = 31s   C = 21s   Done = 25.5s
SERIAL FRACTION (A+B + C, both single-threaded) = 52s of 78.7s = 66.1%     (was 68%)
JVM on the same box and affinity: wall 6.7s   cpu 20.8s
rava cpu 142s = 6.8x the JVM's machine work
```

⚠ Read the RATIO, not the absolute. This harness arms phase instrumentation to split A+B/C/Done, so
its 78.7s is inflated against the 66.5s the uninstrumented A/B batches read. The fraction is
uniform across arms and is the number to use.

⇒ Scaled onto the real 66.5s wall, the serial blocks are **~44s**. **Even with Done at ZERO, wall
cannot go below ~44s**, against a 20s target. A whole session of work moved wall 35% and Done 55%
and left this ratio untouched — which is the point: the serial fraction is not something the
micro-seam can reach. And cpu is still **6.8x** the JVM's for the same boot, the same gap recorded
months ago.

## The one-line diagnosis, measured

`RAVA_PROFILE_PC` on the current tree, all four boot blocks:

```
host side 95.2% / 89.5% / 92.6% / 93.6% of wall
```

⇒ **Compiled machine code executes only ~5-10% of the boot.** The other 90% is rava's own Rust -
the interpreter and the native JDK layer - executing guest semantics. That is not a defect to be
found in a profile; it is the consequence of implementing the JDK as Rust natives, which is a
deliberate design choice (see the no-adapt rule: generic JDK natives, never per-jar shims).

So `wall < 20s` is not a question of finding the next hot spot. It asks for one of:
  * the same guest semantics executed as COMPILED CODE rather than by our Rust, which is option 1
    below and is gated on object representation, or
  * the Rust natives themselves being ~3x faster, which after this session's sweep of that seam
    (six memos refuted, two allocation removals null, one shipped) looks like a rewrite rather
    than a series of fixes, or
  * the serial blocks running in parallel, which prior work recorded as blocked - and note the
    lane's own curve says four workers is optimal and more is worse, so this is about making A+B
    and C parallel at all, not about widening the ring.

## ⚠ The harness had a 1.85% bias, and it cost one of the claims above

An A/A control — the IDENTICAL binary in both arms — returned `Done −1.85% mean, −2.9% min`, with
the "winner" ahead in every sorted position on both metrics. Cause: the pair order was randomised
but not BALANCED, and the first run of a pair is systematically slower (world restore just
finished, cold page cache, unsettled CPU). `two_exe_ab.ps1` now alternates strictly.

Re-measuring the worker env gates under alternation took them from **−3.62% to −0.31%** on Done
means. The change stays — it removes a locked syscall and the counted evidence for the
environment-block lock serialising workers stands — but the percentage does not.

⇒ **Run an A/A control before trusting an A/B on this box; ~2% of Done means is the floor.**
Results that survive it are the ON CLEAN ones, where every run of one arm beat every run of the
other across two batches with reversed order: the gauntlet shortcut (wall −3.1%) and the map-key
derivation (Done −6.1%). `boot_flag_ab.ps1` sequences were already balanced ABBA, so the flag A/Bs
(including argument-buffer recycling) are not affected by this bias.

## 2026-07-29, later: what the SERIAL window actually is, by GUEST method

The host-symbol profile is flat. The guest-method profile of the same time is not:

```
block t=12.5s   WallBlock.lambda$makeShapes$0             34.6%
                StateHolder.lambda$populateNeighbours$0   23.0%
                <vm>.cranelift-compile                    14.0%
                CrossCollisionBlock.lambda$makeShapes$1    5.0%
block t=24.9s   BlockBehaviour$BlockStateBase.initCache()  60.5%
```

⇒ **~60% of the serial window is three PER-BLOCK-STATE loops** over MC's ~26k states: shape
building, the neighbour table, cache init. Each element is independent work. The host profile
looked flat only because that work is spread over hundreds of small Rust helpers.
★ **The lens decides the conclusion**: "which of our code is hot" said *nothing is*; "what is the
program doing" says *three embarrassingly-parallel loops*. Run both before calling a seam exhausted.

### And the parallel blocker, now named precisely

`RAVA_FORK_SHAPES` DOES fire on a real boot and DOES reach the right place - the trace ends at
`StateDefinition.lambda$new$3 cap=5 candidate=false`. It is rejected on a principled rule: the
fork-each probe admits only ELEMENT-OWNERSHIP consumers - an unbound `Element::m` or a static
`m(Element)`, where the element is the private receiver. MC's per-state lambdas capture the shared
accumulators they are filling (`Map`, `List`, `List` in that descriptor), so they are not
element-owned and forking them as-is would be unsound.

### ⛔ The stream-map fork is refuted by SIZE - measured, not argued

The shape loops are invisible to the fork probes, and the reason is NOT that they are compiled: MC
builds shapes with `.stream().map(..).collect(..)`, and the probes match a classic `iterator()` +
hasNext/next loop. That looked promising, because the stream `map` loop is OURS (`stream.rs`), so
forking it would need no bytecode analysis of the caller at all - only a decision about the mapper.

A census of that loop (`RAVA_STREAM_MAP_STAT`, default OFF) closes it:

```
150,000 calls, 505,923 elements (3.4 per call)
n<4: 123,428   n<16: 19,843   n<64: 6,729   n<256: 0   n>=256: 0
```

**Not one stream map in the boot has 64 elements or more, and 82% have fewer than four.** No fork
overhead amortises over four lambda calls. The pipeline count is large and every pipeline is tiny.

★ This check cost one turn. The equivalent check on the ITERATOR fork was not done until four turns
of blocker analysis had already been spent - and it too ended in a ceiling (~15%). **Size the prize
first; a blocker analysis is only worth doing on a lever whose prize you have already measured.**

⚠ The first version of this census was itself defective, which is worth remembering: it bucketed on
`fork_min_n()` (default 2, so "big" meant nothing), labelled mappers with `value_class_name` (which
returns the generic `$Lambda` for every lambda), and cost enough per call to take the boot to 149s.
A census must be cheap enough that the run it measures is still the run you meant.

### SIZE THE PRIZE BEFORE STARTING: perfect parallelisation of all three loops leaves wall at ~55s

Done before committing anyone to a multi-session analysis project, because it changes whether the
project is worth starting.

The two profiled blocks span roughly 25s of the boot and the three per-state loops are ~60% of them,
so about **15s of guest work**. Parallelised PERFECTLY at the lane's measured optimum of four
workers: 15s -> ~3.8s, saving **~11s**.

```
wall 66.5s - 11s  ~=  55s          target: 20s
```

⇒ **Even a flawless fork of everything identified leaves wall ~2.75x above the target.** It is a
worthwhile 15%, and it is not the goal. This agrees with the independent serial-fraction
arithmetic (serial ~44s of 66.5s, unchanged by a session that moved wall 35%): no single lever
removes more than about a third of the serial window.

⇒ So `wall < 20s` needs the parallel work AND the 6.8x CPU gap against the JVM closed - the two are
not alternatives. Anyone starting the fork project should start it as a 15% improvement with a hard
ceiling, not as the path to the target.

### The 60% is TWO targets with TWO DIFFERENT blockers - verified, not assumed

| target | share | seen by a fork probe? | blocker |
|---|---|---|---|
| `BlockStateBase.initCache()` | 60.5% of its block | **YES** - 1943 trace lines, shape ADMITTED | whole-program interface closure (below) |
| `WallBlock.lambda$makeShapes$0` + `StateHolder.lambda$populateNeighbours$0` | 57.6% of its block | **NO - ZERO occurrences** in a 38,357-line trace | the fork detectors live in the INTERPRETER; these loops run COMPILED, so nothing ever looks at them |

The second row is not a refusal, it is an absence. `Block.lambda$getShapeForEachState$13` is compiled
(`seen=204642, compile_ok=1`), and `try_fork_iterator_loop` / the forEach probe are both called from
the interpreter's invoke dispatch. That is the [[rava-g15-fork-target-scan]] finding - "hot worldgen
COMPILED, invisible to interp fork-detectors" - reconfirmed with current numbers.

⇒ So reaching the 60% is TWO pieces of work, not one:
  1. `initCache`: make the offload analysis precise enough at a site (receiver narrowing + a runtime
     guard, per the section below).
  2. `makeShapes`/`populateNeighbours`: fork detection has to exist for COMPILED loops at all. No
     amount of analysis work on (1) touches this one.

### THE SINGLE BLOCKER, drilled to the bottom: `java.lang.Comparable.equals`

`RAVA_OFFLOAD_DRILL` prints the rejection chain. All 777 skips of the initCache loop are one chain,
and it bottoms out in one place:

```
BlockState.initCache()
  -> Block.getFluidState(BlockState)              46 concrete targets, 45 FAILING
    -> FlowingFluid.getSource(Z)                  1 target: LavaFluid$Source
      -> FluidState.setValue(Property, Comparable)
        -> StateHolder.setValueInternal(...)
          -> java/lang/Comparable.equals(Object)
             UNENUMERABLE: declared owner UNLOADABLE [no pure native contract]
             iface-closure(Gate-1): 186 loaded concrete targets, 82 FAILING
```

⇒ The largest guest cost in the serial window (60.5% of its block) is refused because of ONE
JDK interface method. Two distinct facts are missing, and they need different fixes:

1. **No pure native contract for `Comparable.equals`.** The declared owner is a JDK interface we
   hold no bytecode for, so the closure cannot be enumerated from it at all. The message names the
   shape of the fix itself.
2. **The Gate-1 fallback over-approximates.** Enumerating loaded implementations gives 186 targets
   with 82 failing - but at THIS site the receiver can only be a block-state property VALUE (an
   enum, an Integer, a Boolean), whose `equals` is trivial. The analysis is closing over every
   loaded `Comparable` rather than the types the property can actually hold.

So the refusal is an over-approximation, not a demonstrated hazard - which is the right way round
(GAP-S04: no optimistic relaxation, an unproved class keeps the serial path), but it means the
lever is gated on making the analysis precise here, not on the fork machinery.

**And the over-approximation is STRUCTURAL, which is why this lever has read "blocked" for
sessions.** The drill names the failing targets:

```
iface-closure(Gate-1) java/lang/Comparable.equals -> 186 targets, 82 FAILING
  [37 targets: ExtendedLoggerWrapper, CacheBuilder$2, Excluder, Log4J2Logger, ...] NATIVE [NO-CONTRACT]
  [CubePointRange] -> java/util/List.size() -> UNENUMERABLE
      iface-closure(Gate-1) java/util/List.size() -> 195 targets, 167 FAILING
```

The closure is admitting log4j loggers and guava cache builders as possible receivers of `equals`
inside `StateHolder.setValueInternal`, and then cascading into every loaded `List`. Those can never
be a block-state property value. With a whole-program interface closure over an application this
size, ANY interface call in a fork tree pulls in unrelated classes and fails - so the refusal is
guaranteed in advance and says nothing about `initCache`.

⚠ Note what is NOT the fix: adding a contract for `java/lang/Comparable`. `native_contract`'s own
header forbids it - contracts are keyed by the EXACT dynamic receiver class, "never from a shared
receiver's declared interface" - and the property value types that actually occur here (enums,
`Integer`, `Boolean`, `Character`) ALREADY have contracts. The gap is that the analysis cannot see
which of them reaches this site.

⇒ **The shape that fits this engine: site-level receiver narrowing with a runtime guard.** The PICs
and `RAVA_DEVIRT_PROBE` already record observed receiver classes per site, and the lane already has
region-abort-and-retry-serially. Admitting on observed classes and aborting the region if an
unexpected class appears is optimistic ADMISSION with a sound RUNTIME check - which is exactly the
contract the ring lane already runs under, rather than the static optimism GAP-S04 forbids.

⚠ Do not time a `RAVA_OFFLOAD_DRILL` boot: that run read Done 72.3s because the drill itself is
expensive.

### The initCache loop IS admitted — the missing piece is that the fork runs SERIALLY

The forEach probe rejecting `StateDefinition.lambda$new$3` is a DIFFERENT site. The
ITERATOR-LOOP detector (F3.3) fires on the one that matters:

```
[FORK-ITER-DET] in=net/minecraft/world/level/block/Blocks m=initCache()V   x1166
```

`initCache()V` is a void instance method on the element, i.e. exactly the element-ownership shape
F3.3 admits, it runs through the interpreter so the detector can see it, and it is the single
largest guest cost in the serial window (60.5% of its block). 1166 detections across MC's ~26k
block states is ~22 elements per detected loop - enough to be worth forking.

⚠ Read the trace field correctly: `e=3` in that line is `m.e_local`, the LOCAL SLOT INDEX of the
element variable, NOT an element count. I first read it as "3 elements per loop" and nearly wrote
the lever off as too small. Check what a field means before concluding from it.

⚠ And do not read timings from a `RAVA_FORK_TRACE` run: that boot printed 38,357 `eprintln` lines.

⇒ So for THIS loop the admission is already green and the only missing piece is F3.3's own stated
"next increment" - applying the diverted per-element calls in PARALLEL rather than serially. That is
the first lever of the right size in this ledger whose gate is already open.

⇒ For the makeShapes / populateNeighbours loops, option 3 remains
**"needs per-worker accumulators and a deterministic merge"**.
That is a real design with a real risk (merge order must be fixed or the registry diverges - the
gates exist precisely to catch that), and it is the only remaining option whose target is now named
with numbers. Note also that `try_fork_iterator_loop` still applies its body SERIALLY - its own doc
says the GIL-free parallel execution "is the next increment" and it was never built.

## The two structural options that remain, and their blockers

1. **Emit the hot native operations in MACHINE CODE** instead of answering them in Rust at the
   boundary. `Vm::jit_call_body` is the largest engine symbol (~4%) and it is now mostly the
   shortcut itself. BLOCKER: the iterators and map entries it serves are heap `Ref`s living in a
   Rust-side `ObjectSlot`/`FieldBlob`, whose layout cannot be baked into codegen. Arena objects can
   (`arena_getfield` already exists). So this is gated on migrating those native-born objects into
   the arena — i.e. on the value-model arc, not on the emitter.
2. **Attack the serial fraction itself.** The serial window is **90–95% host-bound** with a FLAT
   leaf tail — nothing above ~4% after this session's work. There is no hot spot left to remove;
   `wall < 20s` needs the engine to stop entering the host, not to enter it more cheaply.

⚠ Measurement discipline that this session had to learn the hard way is in
`bench/two_exe_ab.ps1`, `bench/env_num_sweep.ps1` and `bench/wt_gates.ps1`: a run that does not
reach `Done (...)` is NOT a measurement (eighteen such runs were once reported as timings), order
must be permuted per rep, and `powershell -File` does not parse argument literals — `-Values 3,4,5,6`
silently became the integer 3456 and ran as a worker count.

## Sizing the two remaining populations BEFORE working on them

Applying the rule the stream-map refutation established. Both numbers come from the guest-method
lens, and the first one was then checked against direct instrumentation - which is why it is here.

### Cranelift compile: ~4.5s  ⚠ SEE THE RETRACTION BELOW — the sampler was NOT wrong, my denominator was

`<vm>.cranelift-compile` is in the TOP TWO of every profiled block (14.0% / 11.1% / 20.8% / 16.1%),
which totals 428 of 2892 ticks = **14.8% of the boot**. That would be ~10s of wall, and it is the
largest engine-owned row in the profile.

It is also WRONG. `RAVA_COMPILE_TIME` instruments the compile calls directly and reports:

```
[COMPILE-TIME] 2000 methods compiled, 6.24s cumulative Cranelift compile
   (that run was contended: wall 92.5s / Done 30.4s vs 66.5 / 21.3 clean)
```

Adjusted to a clean boot that is **~4.5s = 6.8% of wall** - and it reproduces the figure already
recorded at `jit.rs:26293` ("6.37s over 2000 compiles on an inflated run, ~4.5s adjusted") to within
2%, on a tree many commits newer. Two independent measurements a long way apart agreeing is a real
number; the sampler's 14.8% is not.

⚠ **WITHDRAWN — see the retraction section.** This paragraph claimed RIP attribution overstated an
engine row by 2x. It did not: method-table rows are shares of JIT_EXEC (43.5% of the run), and I
converted one straight into wall seconds. The original text is left standing below so the mistake
is legible rather than quietly edited away. It read: this is the third lens disagreement of the
cycle (after the host-symbol vs guest-method split, and the bridge census overstating high-count
bridges). The standing rule holds: when a row can be instrumented directly, the sampler's share of
it is a hint, not a measurement.

So the prize is 4.5s, and only PART of it is recoverable - a background compiler thread does not
delete the work, it moves it, and the main thread runs interpreted until the code is published.
Realistically ~2-3s, i.e. **~4% of wall**.

The BLOCKER, however, has shrunk, and the doc at `jit.rs:26293` is now out of date: it names
`Cell<bool> initialized` as one of three, but `LoadedClass` already carries `AtomicBool` for

and `site_cache: RefCell` - across **20 and 2 borrow sites**. And neither is hot: the getstatic fast

converting these to `RwLock` does not touch the path that once paid Done -31%. This is also exactly
the direction `feat/vm-shared-exec` is already going.

### Mojang codec decoding  ⛔ SUPERSEDED: this says ~7.3s; corrected to ~3.0s in the retraction below

Blocks 3 and 4 are not the ring - they are datapack/registry DECODE, and this cycle never looked at

```
MapDecoder.lambda$compressedDecode$1   16.7%
KeyDispatchCodec.lambda$decode$2        7.0%
ListCodec$DecoderState.accept           6.8%
Decoder$1.lambda$decode$1               4.6%
```

Blocks 3+4 are 1430 of 2892 ticks (49% of the boot), and codec rows are ~38% of block 4 and ~8% of

Note this is NOT the closed codec-flatten arc (`rava-codec-flatten-generator`, closed low-yield

### What the sum says about `wall < 20s`

Everything identified and not refuted, at its CEILING and assuming perfect recovery:

| lever | ceiling | state |
|---|---|---|
| codec decode | ~~7.3s~~ **~3.0s** (corrected) | mechanism named; the obvious lever is a refuted null |
| Cranelift compile offload | ~4.5s (realistic ~2-3s) | ✅ UNBLOCKED - inputs are type-verified `Send` |
| the three per-state loops | ~11s | two hard blockers, documented above |

Sum of ceilings ~19s against a 66.5s wall = **~28%**, landing at ~48s. Every one of those is a
ceiling, not an estimate, and two of the three are blocked. The target is 20s.

**So `wall < 20s` is not reachable by the sum of every lever currently identified**, and that is now
an arithmetic statement over measured numbers rather than an impression. Reaching it requires the
engine to stop being 6.8x the JVM's machine work per boot - the value-model arc - not another pass
over this seam.

## The last `!Sync` field is type-level EASY and semantics-level open

`site_cache` is gone (commit `9955b31`), so `LoadedClass` has exactly one `!Sync` field left:
`statics: RefCell<FastMap<String, Value>>`. The note at `jit.rs` calls it "the hard one — a RefCell
of guest `Value`s is the GIL problem in miniature, not a lock that can simply be swapped in".

That is right about the SEMANTICS and wrong about the TYPES, and the two were being conflated.
`Value` is `Int | Long | Float | Double | Str(Arc<str>) | Ref(u32) | Array(u32) | Obj(ArenaPtr) |
Null | StdOut | StdErr` — primitives, an `Arc<str>`, plain handles, and an `ArenaPtr` that already
carries `unsafe impl Send + Sync`. So **`Value` is already `Send + Sync`**, and
`RwLock<FastMap<String, Value>>` compiles to a `Sync` `LoadedClass` with no new unsafe.

What the note is actually pointing at is that making the map REACHABLE from two threads is not the
same as making concurrent static reads/writes CORRECT under the GIL-free lane. That is a real
question and it is separate from the type change.

Cost to watch when it is done: the field doc records that `getstatic` consults this map BY NAME and
that SipHashing those Strings was 1.9% of wall (which is why it is `FastMap`). An `RwLock` read adds
two atomics on top of a hash and a probe, so the honest expectation is a small REGRESSION on that
path, to be bought back by what it unblocks. It must be A/B'd on its own, not bundled.

### Correction: there were FOUR blockers, not one, and only the compiler knew

The section above says `statics` is the last `!Sync` field. It was wrong, and the way it was wrong
is the reusable part.

Converting `statics` to `RwLock` and enabling `assert_send::<InlineCallee>()` did NOT compile:

```
error[E0277]: `OnceCell<HashMap<Box<str>, Vec<(Box<str>, usize)>, …>>` cannot be shared
   = help: within `LoadedClass`, the trait `Sync` is not implemented for `OnceCell<…>`
   note: required because it appears within the type `ClassFile`      <- NOT LoadedClass
   note: required because it appears within the type `LoadedClass`
```

`ClassFile::method_lookup` — a lazy method-resolution map in `rava-classfile`, a DIFFERENT CRATE.
`LoadedClass` embeds `ClassFile`, so a `!Sync` field there blocks `Arc<LoadedClass>: Send` exactly
as one declared in `LoadedClass` would. Every previous round of this — including mine — enumerated
`LoadedClass`'s OWN fields and reported "the last blocker is X" three times running.

★ **A structural claim about a type is only as good as the compiler check that backs it.** Reading
fields off a struct definition cannot see what it embeds. The fix was `cell::OnceCell` →
`sync::OnceLock` (set once, read many, value a pure function of the immutable method table, so a
race just recomputes an identical map) — one line, parked behind three wrong inventories.

STATE NOW: `assert_send::<InlineCallee>()` compiles, 412 tests pass. The Cranelift compile inputs
are `Send`, so the ~4.5s background-compile lever is no longer type-blocked. What is NOT settled,
and is not claimed: whether concurrent static access is CORRECT under the GIL-free lane. Type
reachability from two threads is not thread-safety of the guest program.

## The codec population's mechanism, and why the obvious lever is already refuted

The ~7.3s of Mojang codec decode is lambda-dense by construction — `MapDecoder.lambda$compressedDecode$1`,
`KeyDispatchCodec.lambda$decode$2`, `Decoder$1.lambda$decode$1` are the top self-time rows — and
`Vm::heappic_fill` rejects those receivers OUTRIGHT:

```rust
Some(c) if c.starts_with('$') || c.starts_with("java/") => { note_fill(true); return; }
```

A `$`-synthetic (lambda) or `java/` receiver class is PERMANENTLY NeverCacheable. So every
functional-interface call inside the codec pipeline is a guaranteed PIC miss that falls to the host.
That is a real mechanism and it explains the population's shape.

⛔ **It is nevertheless not a lever, and the refutation is already in this tree.** The direct-mapped
dispatch table turned 35,018,916 host callbacks into machine-code hits and lifted PIC coverage from
39.3% to 45.9% — removing 12.6% of ALL PIC misses — and was worth ZERO (Done +1.7%, overlapping;
wall marginally worse). That is where the standing rule came from: **counting host callbacks is not
a way to price host time**, which invalidated the "290M × ~99ns ≈ 29s" sizing that made this whole
family of levers look large.

So "make lambda receivers cacheable" is a re-run of a measured null, not a new idea, and the
~99ns-per-fall price model that would justify it is refuted. If the codec population is to be
attacked, it needs a mechanism that removes WORK (as the key-intern and REF_STATIC_CELLS wins did),
not one that relocates a dispatch.

## RETRACTION: "the sampler was 2x wrong" — it was not. The DENOMINATOR was wrong.

Two sections above claim the RIP sampler overstated `<vm>.cranelift-compile` by 2x (14.8% against a
directly-instrumented ~4.5s). That claim is WITHDRAWN, and it was my arithmetic, not the tool's.

The method table's header says what its denominator is and I read past it:

```
[WALL-METHOD running TOTAL] top-20 methods by self-time RUN-TO-DATE (3067 JIT_EXEC ticks attributed)
[WALL-PROFILE]     43.5%      3131  JIT_EXEC (Cranelift machine code)
```

**Method shares are shares of JIT_EXEC, not of wall**, and JIT_EXEC is 43.5% of the run. Converting
a row straight into seconds of boot double-counts by 1/0.435 ≈ 2.3x — which is exactly the "2x
discrepancy" I attributed to the sampler.

Redone properly:

| row | of JIT_EXEC | x 43.5% = of wall | seconds at 66.5s | independent check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `<vm>.cranelift-compile` | 428/3067 = 14.0% | 6.1% | **~4.0s** | `RAVA_COMPILE_TIME` ~4.5s ✓ |
| Mojang codec decode | 319/3067 = 10.4% | 4.5% | **~3.0s** | — |

The two lenses AGREE to within 12% once the denominator is right. The sampler is not the unreliable
instrument here.

⇒ **The codec population is ~3.0s, not the ~7.3s recorded above.** It is therefore SMALLER than the
compile lever, not "half again bigger", and the section claiming otherwise is superseded.

## And "self-time" in that table is ENTRY self-time — it does not mean own work

`rava_sampler::CURRENT_METHOD` is stored by `jit_method_push/pop` at COMPILED ENTRY only. Its own
doc: "a machine-code PIC / direct-mono hit jumps straight to the callee and is deliberately
invisible here; billing it to the entry frame is the whole point of entry self-time".

So a row is "ticks whose innermost COMPILED ENTRY was this method", including everything it reached
through the PIC. The partition is sound (each tick lands on exactly one entry, push/pop restores),
but "self" must not be read as "this method's own instructions".

This killed a lever before it was built. `MapDecoder.lambda$compressedDecode$1` carries 16.7% of a
block, and `javap` shows its entire body is:

```
aload_0; aload_1; aload_2; invokeinterface decode(…); areturn
```

A five-bytecode forwarder cannot cost 16.7% of anything. It is simply the last host-visible entry,
so the whole `decode` subtree bills to it. The lever this suggested — collapse trivial forwarder
lambdas, a generic shape (`analyze_trivial_getter` exists; no forwarder equivalent does) — would
therefore remove a frame and NOT the time under it. Refuted before a line was written, by reading
what the number meant.

★ The rule this session keeps re-learning, now in its sharpest form: **before converting a profiler
row into seconds, read what the row is a share OF.** Three of this cycle's four "lens disagreements"
were the same mistake, not three different instruments lying.

## NATIVE_BRIDGES decomposed at last — and it is two-thirds WAITING, one-third FLAT

NATIVE_BRIDGES is the second-largest category of the serial window (~21%, against JIT_EXEC's ~60%)
and had never been broken down: the method table is scoped to JIT_EXEC ticks by construction, so
every bridge tick fell outside every row it prints. The existing census (`RAVA_BRIDGE_STAT`) TIMES
each entry, which overstates high-count/low-work bridges — the `charAt` scar. So the category was
re-instrumented by SAMPLING (`CURRENT_BRIDGE`, same design as `CURRENT_METHOD`), and measured:

```
[WALL-BRIDGE TOTAL] 4082 NATIVE_BRIDGES ticks
  66.1%  java/util/concurrent/CompletableFuture#allOf     <- 98% of the FINAL block
   5.0%  java/util/Map#get
   1.8%  it/unimi/.../Reference2ObjectMap#reference2ObjectEntrySet
   1.3%  java/lang/Object#equals
   1.3%  java/nio/file/Files#newInputStream
   1.0%  java/util/stream/Stream#map
   0.8%  java/util/List#sort
   0.6%  <gson>#tokenize+parse
```

**Two thirds of the category is the main thread PARKED in `allOf` waiting for the ring.** That is
not cost — removing it cannot speed anything up, it is the shape of a thread waiting. It also
confirms, and now quantifies, the standing note that the whole-run NATIVE_BRIDGES figure is
parking rather than work.

The remaining third is FLAT. The largest genuine bridge is `Map#get` at 5.0% of the category =
~2.2% of wall. And `<gson>#tokenize+parse` — the bridge the category is NAMED after
("NATIVE_BRIDGES (gson/R2OMAP/IO)") — is **0.6%**, so the label is now actively misleading about
where the time goes.

⇒ **NATIVE_BRIDGES is not a lever.** The largest un-decomposed population on the board closes with
no target in it, and the flat-tail diagnosis now holds under a THIRD independent instrument (host
symbols, guest methods, and now bridges).

★ Worth noting what this cost: the answer came from ~60 lines of sampling, not from an experiment.
The category had carried a suggestive name and a plausible size for the whole cycle without anyone
asking what was inside it.

## What is actually IN the JIT_EXEC bucket (the recorded shorthand is imprecise)

The standing note says the sampler's JIT_EXEC guard "wraps ALL of `jit_run`". Read the site
(`lib.rs`, the `run_const` call) and it does not — it wraps exactly the machine-code invocation:

```rust
let bits = {
    let _wp = crate::rava_sampler::enter(crate::rava_sampler::JIT_EXEC);
    f(cells.as_mut_ptr(), consts_ptr)
};
```

The conclusion survives, but for a sharper reason. Guards are a swap-and-restore stack, so anything
called from compiled code that RE-CATEGORISES itself leaves the bucket — native bridges push
NATIVE_BRIDGES, interpreter re-entry pushes INTERP_EXEC. What stays billed to JIT_EXEC is the
machine code PLUS every piece of host machinery that does NOT re-categorise: dispatch resolution,
allocation, GC, the PIC miss path.

⇒ **JIT_EXEC is not "time inside compiled code".** It is "compiled code plus its uncategorised host
tail", and the two can differ by a large factor. That is why a codegen lever can be real and still
measure 2-6%: it acts only on the first term, and only the RIP split
(`bench/inside_compiled.ps1`) says how big that term is.

★ This also explains the shape of the whole cycle without needing any lever to be "wrong": the
value-model flip (5.6% of emitted ops at best), the dispatch diamonds (halving them, −2.6%) and the
instruction-bloat work all act on the same first term. If that term is small, their measured sizes
are not disappointing — they are arithmetic.

## Pre-registered: what JIT_CALLBACK must show, and the conflict it has to resolve

Written BEFORE the measurement, so the reading is not fitted to the result afterwards.

`jit_call` armed no sampler category, so a PIC miss taken out of compiled code stayed billed to
JIT_EXEC for its whole host excursion. `JIT_CALLBACK` now splits it out. Two outcomes, and they
mean opposite things:

* **JIT_CALLBACK is LARGE (say 30-45% of the serial window).** Then JIT_EXEC's ~60% was mostly host
  dispatch, every codegen lever has been acting on a ~20% slice, and their uniform 2-6% results are
  arithmetic rather than disappointment. The host dispatch path would be ~18s of a 66.5s boot —
  the first goal-SIZED quantity this cycle has found.
* **JIT_CALLBACK is SMALL (<10%).** Then compiled machine code really is ~60% of the serial window,
  the codegen levers were aimed correctly and simply are not worth much, and the 6.6x CPU gap is in
  the emitted code's quality after all.

### The conflict either outcome must face

A LARGE result contradicts a measurement already in the tree. `RAVA_DISPATCH_TABLE` was built: it
turned 35,018,916 host callbacks into machine-code hits and lifted PIC coverage 39.3% → 45.9%,
removing **12.6% of all PIC misses** — and it was worth ZERO (Done +1.7%, overlapping; wall
marginally worse). If misses were 40% of the serial window, removing an eighth of them should have
paid ~5%.

Three reconciliations, and the measurement plus a follow-up must pick one rather than leaving it
open:

1. **The table's own emitted probe cost cancelled its win** — it added two loads and a branch to
   every dispatch site to save a subset of misses. Testable: compare block counts per call and
   `Done` with the table armed but its fills disabled.
2. **The removed misses were the cheap ones.** The table serves monomorphic-ish sites; the
   expensive misses may be the ~39 megamorphic sites. Testable: bucket JIT_CALLBACK ticks by site
   arity.
3. **JIT_CALLBACK is small** and there is no conflict — the dispatch-table null was simply correct.

⚠ Note what CANNOT be concluded either way: JIT_CALLBACK is a TIME share, while the dispatch-table
work counted CALLBACKS. This tree already established that counting host callbacks is not a way to
price host time. That is precisely why the category was added — to price the same population in the
unit that matters.

## RESULT: JIT_CALLBACK is 31.7% of the serial window — the largest single category, bigger than machine code

The pre-registered LARGE outcome, and larger than the range it named.

```
SERIAL WINDOW (first dump)              WHOLE RUN (final dump)
  31.7%  JIT_CALLBACK (PIC miss)         30.3%  JIT_CALLBACK (PIC miss)
  28.5%  JIT_EXEC (machine code)         30.2%  JIT_EXEC (machine code)
  24.5%  NATIVE_BRIDGES                  22.5%  NATIVE_BRIDGES
  11.9%  INTERP_EXEC                     12.1%  INTERP_EXEC
   2.7%  VM_DISPATCH                      4.2%  VM_DISPATCH
   0.6%  CLASS_LOADING                    0.7%  CLASS_LOADING
```

**The row that read "JIT_EXEC (Cranelift machine code) ~60%" was about HALF machine code and half
the host excursion taken on a PIC miss.** Splitting it needed one guard on `Vm::jit_call`, which
had armed no category at all.

### What this settles

Every codegen lever this cycle priced — the value-model flip (5.6% of emitted ops on its best
possible workload), halving the dispatch diamonds (−2.6%), the instruction-bloat work — acts only
on the machine-code term. That term is **28.5% of the serial window, not 60%**. Their uniform 2-6%
results were never disappointing; they were arithmetic against a denominator that was twice too
big. Nothing about those measurements was wrong, and nothing about the levers was weak — the model
of what they could reach was wrong, and had been since the categories were first defined.

★ The whole cycle's shape follows from one unguarded call site.

### And the first goal-sized quantity on the board

JIT_CALLBACK is ~30% of the boot — order 20s of a 66.5s wall. Every other candidate measured this
cycle tops out at ~4.5s. It is the only quantity found that is large enough to matter for
`wall < 20s`.

### The pre-registered conflict is now live, and must be resolved before anyone builds

`RAVA_DISPATCH_TABLE` removed **12.6% of all PIC misses** (35,018,916 host callbacks became
machine-code hits, PIC coverage 39.3% → 45.9%) and was worth **ZERO** — Done +1.7% overlapping,
wall marginally worse. If misses are 30% of the run, removing an eighth of them should have paid
~3.8%.

Two live reconciliations (the third, "JIT_CALLBACK is small", is refuted):

1. **The table's own emitted probe cancelled its win** — two loads and a branch added to EVERY
   dispatch site to serve a subset of misses.
2. **The removed misses were the cheap ones.** The table serves monomorphic-ish sites; the ~39
   megamorphic sites may carry most of the time.

⚠ Do not treat "JIT_CALLBACK is 30%" as "a dispatch fix is worth 30%". The dispatch-table null is a
measured counterexample to exactly that inference, on exactly this population. The next step is to
find out WHICH misses hold the time — bucket JIT_CALLBACK ticks by site arity — not to build
another dispatch mechanism on the strength of a category total.

## RESOLVED: the PIC-miss time is CONCENTRATED, and it is concentrated on LAMBDA receivers

Per-site attribution of JIT_CALLBACK (`[WALL-SITE]`, published from `jit_call` as a raw
(caller class, cp) pair, aggregated by the sampler). Serial window:

```
top-20 of 125 distinct sites hold 70.5% of JIT_CALLBACK
  18.9%  IndirectMerger           @cp48  -> IndexMerger$IndexConsumer.merge(III)Z
  12.3%  DiscreteCubeMerger       @cp41  -> IndexMerger$IndexConsumer.merge(III)Z
   5.2%  Shapes                   @cp141 -> BooleanOp.apply(ZZ)Z
   3.0%  BitSetDiscreteVoxelShape @cp166 -> BooleanOp.apply(ZZ)Z
   1.2%  WallBlock                @cp109 -> Function.apply(…)
```

**TWO sites calling the same method hold 31.2% of the category** — about 9.9% of the serial window,
order 4.5s of a 66.5s boot. The tail is 125 sites, not thousands.

`IndexConsumer`, `BooleanOp`, `Function`, `BiFunction` are all FUNCTIONAL INTERFACES, so the
receiver is a lambda, whose class name begins with `$`. And `Vm::heappic_fill` refuses those
outright:

```rust
Some(c) if c.starts_with('$') || c.starts_with("java/") => { note_fill(true); return; }
```

⇒ These calls miss the PIC **by rule, not by circumstance**. Every one of them takes the host
excursion, forever, however hot the site gets.

### This resolves the pre-registered conflict — reconciliation #2 wins

`RAVA_DISPATCH_TABLE` removed 12.6% of all PIC misses for ZERO. It keys on `class_id`, but lambda
receivers are rejected by the `$`-prefix test BEFORE any table could serve them, so it never
covered these sites at all. **The misses it removed were the cheap ones**, exactly as
reconciliation #2 predicted. The null was correct and is not evidence against attacking the
population — it measured a different part of it.

### Why this is new rather than a re-run

The `$Lambda` rejection was already known, and lambda-PIC work is recorded as refuted
(`lambda-impl-key` NEUTRAL, `docs/lambda-machine-code-pic-blocker.md`). What is new is the UNIT.
Every prior justification and refutation of a lambda-dispatch lever was argued on CALLBACK COUNTS
or on synthetic gates (ChunkFill, RingScan) — and this tree's own rule says counting host callbacks
is not a way to price host time. This is the first time the population has been priced in TIME, on
the real boot, per site. It says two sites are worth ~4.5s.

⚠ Which does NOT mean a lambda PIC is worth 4.5s. It means the prize is that large IF the calls can
be served without the excursion. The recorded blocker must be read before anything is built — and
the previous refutations must be re-read for what they actually measured, since at least one of
them (`lambda-impl-key`) was measured on a gate that may not even exercise these sites.

## CORRECTION: JIT_CALLBACK was billing the CALLEE'S BODY, not just the boundary

The two sections above are wrong in their headline numbers, and the cause was checkable at a call
site. `Vm::jit_direct_invoke` reaches the compiled callee like this:

```rust
let bits = unsafe { jit::call_raw(fptr as *const u8, cells, desc_cell) };   // no JIT_EXEC guard
```

No category is armed, so the callee's ENTIRE compiled body was billed to the JIT_CALLBACK excursion
that reached it. And this is not a corner: the recorded lambda blocker measures that **92% of all
lambda host falls are served by this very path** against a warm per-site direct cache. So a category
introduced to measure the boundary tax was reading boundary tax PLUS every body it dispatched to.

Guarded, and re-measured on the same boot shape:

```
                             BEFORE (wrong)      AFTER (correct)
JIT_EXEC (machine code)          28.5%               39.1%
JIT_CALLBACK (PIC miss)          31.7%               20.4%
NATIVE_BRIDGES                   24.5%               25.8%
INTERP_EXEC                      11.9%               10.9%
```

### What has to be withdrawn

* ⛔ **"The JIT_EXEC row was about half machine code and half the PIC-miss host path."** No. Machine
  code is 39.1% of the serial window and the boundary tax is 20.4%. Splitting the row was still
  right and still worth doing — the old 60% really was two different things — but the split is
  roughly 2:1, not 1:1.
* ⛔ **"Two sites hold 31.2% of the category, order 4.5s."** With bodies attributed correctly the
  two merge sites hold **15.2%** of JIT_CALLBACK ≈ 3.1% of the serial window ≈ **1.4s**, not 4.5s.
* ✅ **What survives:** the population is concentrated (124 sites, top-20 hold 60.8%), it is
  dominated by lambda/functional-interface receivers, and the dispatch-table null is still explained
  by those receivers being refused before any class_id table could serve them.

### The corrected figure agrees with the pricing already in the tree

`docs/lambda-machine-code-pic-blocker.md` measured a warm directable-lambda fall at **~99 ns** and
found that removing 1,411,977 of them was worth **−2.3%**. A boundary tax of 1.4s across the two
hottest sites is the same order. The 4.5s claim contradicted an existing measurement, which is
exactly the check that should have been run before publishing it.

★ Third time this cycle the same failure mode has produced a wrong headline: **a profiler bucket
includes whatever it dispatches into unless something re-categorises.** The method table
(`CURRENT_METHOD`) documents this for PIC-resolved callees, and I still walked into it twice more —
once reading entry self-time as own work, once here. The rule is not "be careful with profilers";
it is **find the call site that arms the bucket and read what it encloses, before quoting a number
from it.**

## STATE AFTER THE 2026-07-29 PROFILING SESSION

```
39.1%  JIT_EXEC        Cranelift machine code
25.8%  NATIVE_BRIDGES  two-thirds of it is the main thread PARKED in CompletableFuture#allOf
20.4%  JIT_CALLBACK    PIC miss -> host dispatch; 124 sites, top-20 hold 60.8%
10.9%  INTERP_EXEC
 3.1%  VM_DISPATCH
```

### The rule this session paid for four times

**A profiler bucket contains whatever it dispatches into, unless something re-categorises.** It
cost: entry self-time read as own work; a JIT_EXEC share converted straight into wall seconds; and
JIT_CALLBACK billing whole callee bodies until `jit_direct_invoke`'s bare `call_raw` was found. The

encloses, before quoting a number from it.**

## A CANDIDATE WITH A MECHANISM: the entry-set materializer re-builds the whole map 460,514 times

Hunting a reliable wall reduction, three hypotheses were sized before any был built. Two died on
count alone, which is the cheap half of the "size the prize first" rule working:

* **identity-map key formatting** (`MapKey::str(format!("@{h}"))`): fewer than 5M derivations on a
  whole boot — the probe never printed. Refuted before the fix was written.
* **structural key TEXT volume**: 750,000 structural keys totalling 10,026,531 bytes = **13 bytes
  average**. Nothing like the 21 MB-per-call pathology this tree once found. Whole `map_key`
  population is 1M ops (identity 1,468 / combo 490,222 / structural 508,310).

The third survives, and TWO independent instruments agree on it:

```
[BRIDGE-STAT] self=1.98s  460,514 calls  java/util/Map#get
[BRIDGE-STAT] self=0.87s  460,514 calls  Reference2ObjectMap#reference2ObjectEntrySet
[WALL-BRIDGE] 30.2% of block A+B bridge ticks  java/util/Map#get      (sampled, ≈2.0s)
[WALL-BRIDGE] 11.0%                            reference2ObjectEntrySet
```

Identical call counts, and the sampled and timed views land on the same ~2s for `Map#get` — the
first time in this cycle two instruments have agreed on a bridge without correction.

### The mechanism, read at the site

`map.rs`'s entry-set arm, per CALL:

```rust
let entries = drain_any(vm, &recv);              // drain the WHOLE map
… .map(|(k, val)| {
    let e = vm.heap.alloc("java/util/Map$Entry");  // a fresh GUEST object per entry
    vm.heap.put_field(e, "$key", k);
    vm.heap.put_field(e, "$val", val);
})
```

So each of the 460,514 calls re-materialises the entire map as new guest objects, plus a collection
object. At 4-8 properties per block state that is millions of short-lived guest allocations, and
the 0.87s is only the direct time — the GC pressure lands elsewhere.

This sits inside the boot's top guest row: `BlockStateBase.initCache` (22.9% of block A+B's
JIT_EXEC) and `populateNeighbours` (10.1%).

### Why this is a better shape than the levers this cycle refuted

It REMOVES work rather than relocating a dispatch, and it is not a cache in front of an
already-short path: the path is ~1.9 us per call. A block-state property map is built once and then
read, so the same materialisation is repeated identically hundreds of thousands of times.

⚠ NOT YET a win — only a sized, mechanised candidate. The prize is bounded by 2.9s of a ~75s boot
(~3.9%) and the real number could be lower if the consumers force materialisation anyway. It must
be built and A/B'd, and this tree has refuted memos before ("interception is the expensive
direction", and one memo measured hits=0 because the wrappers WRITE).

### The caller is pinned: `Reference2ObjectArrayMap`'s COPY CONSTRUCTOR

The per-site table gave the caller class and the exact constant-pool indices, and `javap` turns
those into one method:

```
public Reference2ObjectArrayMap(Reference2ObjectMap<K,V> m)
   2: invokeinterface #56   // m.size()
   7: invokespecial  #61    // this(size)  -> allocates key[] and value[]
  13: invokeinterface #64   // m.reference2ObjectEntrySet()      <- the materialiser
  18: invokeinterface #68   // .iterator()
  25: invokeinterface #74   // hasNext()
  34: invokeinterface #80   // next()
  51: invokeinterface #86   // Entry.getKey()      -> key[i]
  64: invokeinterface #89   // Entry.getValue()    -> value[i]
```

cp 64/68/74/80/86 are exactly the indices the site table ranked. So the population is **460,514
copy-constructions of a block-state property map**, each materialising the source map as guest
`Map$Entry` objects purely to walk them once and throw them away — which is what
`populateNeighbours` does: every neighbouring state copies the property map.

The fast path is therefore ONE native for ONE constructor: read the source's backing arrays, write
two fresh ones. Removed per call: an entry-set materialisation, N guest `Map$Entry` allocations, an
iterator, and 2N+2 bridge crossings.

⚠ CORRECTNESS CRUX: the copy must preserve the source's ITERATION ORDER. Key lookup does not care
(keys are unique), but a later `entrySet()` walk over the COPY is guest-visible, so a reordered
copy could change guest output. The bit-exact gates are what checks this.

⚠ And a process note, because it nearly poisoned this file: the section above was first written
through a shell heredoc that was NOT quoted, so backticks ran as command substitution and javap's
help text was spliced into the ledger. Repaired by reverting the file. Append prose with a QUOTED
heredoc (`<<'EOF'`), never an unquoted one.

### The fast path is BUILT and INERT — the blocker is that the JIT direct-calls the constructor

Both seams exist and both are bit-exact (`ChunkFill 8790f04ace726ecf`, rings `37539c6c375d0c3`), and
a reachability probe (`RAVA_R2O_CTOR_STAT`) proves neither fires: `served=0 declined=0`, and the
census still reads 460,514 `reference2ObjectEntrySet` calls.

What the probe established, in order:

1. **The interpreter seam is never reached.** `opcodes::invokespecial`'s try-native-then-bytecode
   block (the one the fastutil int-set `<init>` already uses) sees none of the 460,514 calls — so
   every caller is COMPILED.
2. **The compiled seam is never reached either.** A `kind == 2` hook at the top of
   `Vm::jit_call_body` also sees none, which means the JIT does not call back at all: it has
   resolved the constructor into its DIRECT-CALL cache and jumps straight to the guest body.

⇒ Serving it requires the JIT to REFUSE that direct call, which is exactly what
`opcodes::force_native_collection` does (`lib.rs`, `kind == 2` → `return None`).

⛔ **And that predicate is granular by NAME, not by descriptor.** Adding `<init>` for this class
disables ALL FIVE of its constructors — including `()V` and `(I)V`, which are what actually
allocate `key[]`/`value[]`. Objects then came out with null arrays and every boot died in seconds
with a log4j provider error. That failure is now understood rather than merely observed; the first
version of this section blamed the seam, and the seam was innocent.

**The next step is therefore one of:**
* serve EVERY `Reference2ObjectArrayMap` constructor natively (`()V` → empty arrays, `(I)V` → two
  `Object[n]`, the copy ctor → copy, and the remaining two by descriptor), so a name-granular
  refusal is safe; or
* make the JIT's kind-2 refusal descriptor-aware, so only the copy constructor loses its direct
  call.

The second is smaller and does not put four more constructors on a native path for no gain.

⚠ The fast path stays in the tree DELIBERATELY INERT rather than being deleted: it is correct,
gate-verified, and its kill switch (`RAVA_NO_R2O_COPY_CTOR`) is wired. But it buys nothing until one
of the two changes above lands, and it must not be counted as a win before then.

### ⛔ REFUTED, and the identification was mine: the copy constructor is called ONCE, not 460,514 times

With the probe printing on its FIRST hit rather than every 50,000:

```
[R2OCTOR] served=0 declined=1
```

**One call on the whole boot, and it declines.** So `Reference2ObjectArrayMap`'s copy constructor is
not the caller of the 460,514 `reference2ObjectEntrySet` materialisations, the fast path built for
it is worthless, and it has been removed from the tree rather than left inert.

### The mistake, precisely

Two instruments, two different populations, joined on a coincidence:

* the **bridge census** counts CALLS at the native boundary: `Map#get` 460,514 and
  `reference2ObjectEntrySet` 460,514 — equal, which read like a signature;
* the **site table** attributes JIT_CALLBACK TIME by call site, and showed
  `Reference2ObjectArrayMap @cp64 -> reference2ObjectEntrySet` at 2.4% of that category.

I read the second as naming the caller of the first. It does not: 2.4% of a time bucket is not
"the source of 460,514 calls", and the equal counts were never evidence that the two rows share a
caller. `javap` then confirmed cp#64 is only in the copy constructor — true, and irrelevant, since
that site is simply not hot.

★ **Equal counts are not a join key.** Two rows agreeing on a number is a hypothesis to test, not a
link to build on — and the test here cost four builds that a first-hit probe would have settled
before any of them.

### What survives, and the instrument the next attempt needs

The population is still real and still unattributed: **460,514 `reference2ObjectEntrySet` calls,
0.87-1.64s self-time**, plus the same count of `Map#get`. What is missing is a CALLER for the
NATIVE BRIDGE rows — the site table only attributes JIT_CALLBACK, and a native bridge is a
different category, so no existing instrument says who calls entrySet.

That is the next thing to build: caller attribution on the bridge table, the same way
`CURRENT_SITE_CLS`/`CP` was added for the PIC-miss category. Until it exists, any claim about who
drives those 460,514 calls is a guess — as this section demonstrates.

## ⛔ THE REFUTATION ABOVE WAS ITSELF WRONG — the copy constructor IS hot

The caller-attribution table (`[BRIDGE-CALLER]`, built precisely because the previous section said
no instrument could name a bridge's caller) settles it on the first run:

```
[BRIDGE-CALLER] top-20 of 120 sites; top-20 hold 72.2% of NATIVE_BRIDGES
  29.7%  StateHolder              @cp199 -> java/util/Map.get
  12.2%  Reference2ObjectArrayMap @cp64  -> reference2ObjectEntrySet
   3.9%  Reference2ObjectArrayMap @cp68  -> ObjectSet.iterator
```

cp#64 is in the COPY CONSTRUCTOR and nowhere else in that class — `javap` confirmed that, and it is
still true. So the constructor runs often enough to hold **12.2% of all native-bridge time** in
block A+B, and reverting the fast path was the wrong call.

### What `served=0 declined=1` actually meant

Not "the constructor is cold". It meant **"my interception point is wrong"**. The probe sat on
`jit_call_body`, which only sees calls that CALL BACK into the host; a constructor the JIT
direct-calls — or inlines, which `ctor_inlines` exists to do — never arrives there. The probe
measured its own seam's reachability, and I read it as measuring the constructor's frequency.

★ A zero from a probe is a statement about the PROBE'S PATH first and about the world second. This
is the same error as the earlier one in mirror image: there I inferred a caller from a coincidence,
here I inferred absence from an instrument that could not have seen it either way.

### Where that leaves the lever

The target is unchanged and now measured twice over: the copy constructor's `entrySet`
materialisation is 12.2% of block A+B's bridge time, and `StateHolder.getValue`'s `Map.get` is
29.7% — together **42% of native-bridge time in the serial block**, both inside the block-state
machinery (`initCache` / `populateNeighbours`).

What is NOT yet known is how to intercept a constructor that never calls back. The next check is
whether `ctor_inlines` admits it — if so, the interception has to happen at INLINE ADMISSION, not
at any call seam, and the fast path already written becomes usable again.

## MEASURED: map-key derivation is ~4.8s of a ~78s boot, at 3,216 ns per 13-byte key

A timer around `map_key` itself — the one funnel every native map operation passes through —
after three separate guesses at why `Map#get` costs ~4.3 us per call were each refuted:

```
[KEYTIME] 1,500,000 derivations, 4.825s total, 3,216 ns avg
[BRIDGE-STAT] self=2.08s  460,514 calls  java/util/Map#get
```

Key derivation is LARGER than the `Map#get` bridge that led me to it, because `put`,
`containsKey` and the rest funnel through the same function. Timer overhead is two
`Instant::now()` per call, ~60 ns against 3,216 — 2%, which does not move the magnitude.

### Why 3,216 ns is the finding

The keys are SMALL: 750,000 structural keys totalling 10,026,531 bytes = **13 bytes average**,
with `BlockState` at 6.3 and `Direction` at 5.0. Building a 13-byte string is tens of nanoseconds.
So ~3.2 us per derivation is **two orders of magnitude more than the work it produces**, and the
cost is the machinery around the string, not the string.

### What has already been ruled out, by measurement

* **identity-map formatting** (`format!("@{h}")`) — under 5M derivations on a whole boot; the probe
  never printed.
* **key TEXT volume** — 13 bytes average, nothing like the 21 MB-per-call pathology once found here.
* **the map class** — the structural payers are `HashMap` (477,338) and `EnumMap` (235,514), not
  the reference-keyed `Reference2ObjectArrayMap` the identity arm exists for.

⇒ The remaining suspects are inside `structural_key_scoped`: the `KeyScope` enter/exit, the
arena-map and ArrayMap admission tests, the `$skey` memo lookup, and whether `value_to_string` runs
GUEST bytecode for an object key. That is the next split to time, and it is one funnel with a
handful of branches rather than a search.

★ This is the first quantity in this goal measured by a DIRECT TIMER on a single function rather
than inferred from category shares — which matters, because every share-derived number in this
cycle needed a correction and this one needs none.

## The mechanism inside the 4.8s: the "alloc-free" combo fold allocates 2N strings per fold

`bench/pcstack_boot.ps1` on `release-diag` names it by caller chain:

```
1.7%  combo_hash_key  < map_key_inner < map_key
1.5%  key_str_mut_in  < structural_key_scoped < combo_hash_of < combo_hash_key
1.1%  drain_map       < structural_key_scoped < combo_hash_of < combo_hash_key
```

and the source is unambiguous:

```rust
fn combo_hash_of(vm: &mut Vm, entries: &[(Value, Value)]) -> u64 {
    for (k, val) in entries {
        let ks = structural_key(vm, k);     // builds a String
        let vs = structural_key(vm, val);   // builds a String
        ph = fnv(ks.as_bytes(), ph); ph = fnv(b"=", ph); ph = fnv(vs.as_bytes(), ph);
    }
}
```

`MapKey::Hash` was introduced as the "alloc-free combo-map key", replacing a canonical
`m:{k=v,…}` String — and it does avoid that ONE string, while still allocating **2N short-lived
Strings per fold** purely to feed their bytes to FNV. At 490,222 folds a boot and a handful of
properties per block state, that is millions of allocations whose only consumer is a hash.

The leaf profile is flat (top row 3.6%), but the key-derivation family sums to ~5-7% of the serial
block, which AGREES with the direct timer's 4.8s of a 78s boot. Two instruments, no correction
needed.

### Two ways to fix it, and their risk is not equal

1. **Stream the same bytes into the hash instead of into a String.** Provably identical output —
   same bytes, same FNV, same u64 — so it cannot change behaviour. But `structural_key` is
   recursive and there is no buffer-writing variant (`key_str_mut_in` also returns `String`), so
   this means either threading a sink through the recursion or writing a second implementation.
   **A second implementation of a key derivation is how two versions silently diverge**, and this
   tree keys guest maps with it.
2. **Memoise the per-VALUE key.** The 490,222 folds recur over a few hundred distinct `Property`
   objects and values, so a per-value memo collapses millions of derivations to hundreds. Cheaper
   to write and impossible to diverge (same function, fewer calls). The risk is the one this tree
   has already been bitten by: a memo whose invalidation is wrong, and one whose hit rate turns out
   to be zero because the values are not as stable as assumed.

⇒ (2) first, because it is verifiable by a hit-rate counter BEFORE it is trusted for time — and a
hit rate of zero is exactly the outcome that killed an earlier memo here, so it must be measured,
not assumed.

## Decomposition of the 4.8s, by direct timers only

| part | measured | per call |
|---|---|---|
| `map_key` TOTAL | **4.8s** over 1.5M derivations | 3,216 ns |
| the combo fold's per-entry `structural_key` | 1.43s over 2M entries | keys 247 ns, values 465 ns |
| the `$idkeys` identity resolution | **0.15s** | 85-102 ns |
| unaccounted remainder | **~3.2s** | — |

### Two hypotheses refuted here, both mine

* **"the fold is the cost"** — it is 1.43s of 4.8s, under a third. The fold matters but does not
  dominate.
* **"the `$idkeys` by-name field lookup is the cost"** — the RIP profile made this look compelling
  (`Heap::get_field` 29.7% on-stack, `field_id_existing` 38.6%, `hash_one<RandomState,str>` 29.1%),
  and it is 0.15s. On-stack percentages are conservative and include stale slots; they rank
  suspects, they do not price them.

### ⚠ And a probe that measured the wrong thing, caught before it was published

The first version of the identity timer was `let _idt = IdKeyTimer::start();` at function scope. A
Drop guard lives to the end of its SCOPE, so it timed all of `map_key` and reported **3,505 ns** —
almost exactly the function's own 3,216 ns, which is what should have given it away. Moved into an
explicit block it reads **102 ns**: a factor of 34 between "what I meant to measure" and "what the
guard actually covered".

★ A scope guard measures its scope. Writing one as a statement-level `let` silently widens it to
the rest of the function, and the result looks like a discovery rather than a mistake.

### What is actually left

~3.2s in the non-combo structural path (508,310 derivations for `HashMap`/`EnumMap` keys) plus the
fold's `drain_arena_array_map` and admission tests. Both are inside `structural_key_scoped`, and
neither has been timed yet. That is the next split — and by now the pattern is clear that it should
be timed rather than reasoned about.

## THE LEVER, located and sized: value-object keys re-run guest `toString()`, 3,028 ns each

The last split closes the decomposition:

| part | measured | per call |
|---|---|---|
| non-combo `structural_key` | **2.42s** over 800,000 | **3,028 ns** |
| the combo fold's per-entry keys | 1.43s over 2M entries | 247 / 465 ns |
| `$idkeys` identity resolution | 0.15s | 85-102 ns |
| `map_key` TOTAL | 4.8s | 3,216 ns |

The same `structural_key` costs 247 ns inside the fold and 3,028 ns outside it — a 12x gap in one
function, and the source says why:

```rust
// Not a drainable map key: route value objects (Identifier, ResourceKey, …)
// through their toString() so equal-by-value keys collide instead of falling to identity
key_str_mut_in(vm, v, salt_mid)
```

`$skey` memoises the derivation **only for keys that are drainable MAPS**. Every other value object
re-runs its guest `toString()` bytecode on every single map operation.

### Why this is the shape a reliable win has

The key population is tiny and hugely repetitive — from the class census:

```
219,520 keys  net/minecraft/world/level/block/state/BlockState
219,142 keys  net/minecraft/core/Direction        <- SIX distinct objects exist
 27,339 keys  net/minecraft/resources/Identifier
  9,712 keys  net/minecraft/resources/ResourceKey$InternKey
```

**219,142 derivations of `Direction` at ~3 us each is ~0.66s spent computing one of six possible
answers.** Memoising cannot change the result — it is the same function, called fewer times — so
unlike every relocation lever this cycle, correctness rests on invalidation alone rather than on a
semantic argument.

### The one real design question: invalidation

`$skey` is currently cleared by map mutators (`put`/`remove`/`clear`). Extending the memo to value
objects means any mutation of such an object must clear it too, i.e. the check belongs in
`Heap::put_field` rather than in the map paths. That is the piece to get right, and the reason to
build it carefully rather than quickly:

* a memo with wrong invalidation is a silent wrong-answer bug, not a slowdown;
* this tree has already shipped one memo whose measured hit rate was ZERO because the values it
  keyed on were being written underneath it.

⇒ Build it with a hit-rate counter and the bit-exact gates, and treat a high hit rate as necessary
but not sufficient — the gates are what prove the answers did not change.

### Serving memo hits without allocating: correct, bit-exact, and worth ~0.08s

`valkey_memo_get` returns `Option<String>`, so a HIT still allocated — pure waste for the fold,
whose only use of the key is to feed its bytes to FNV. `valkey_memo_with` now hands the bytes under
the borrow, and the fold hashes them in place. Byte-identical by construction: same stored key,
same bytes, same FNV, so there is no behaviour to change, and the gates agree (ChunkFill
`8790f04ace726ecf`, rings `37539c6c375d0c3`).

Measured on the funnel timer:

```
before   4.825s   3,216 ns avg
after    4.744s   3,162 ns avg
```

**~0.08s.** Removing 2,000,000 String allocations bought under a tenth of a second — ~1.7% of the
funnel, which is inside this box's run-to-run spread.

★ The same rule again, in a new place: **work removed, counted in units, does not convert to time.**
A short-lived allocation under mimalloc is tens of nanoseconds; two million of them are fractions
of a second, not seconds. The change is kept because it is strictly less work at zero risk — not
because it is a win, and it is recorded as not one.

⇒ What this isolates: the ~3 us per derivation is NOT allocation. It is the guest `toString()`
execution on the non-combo path (2.42s at 3,028 ns over 800,000 calls). Every micro-fix around that
call is worth ~0.1s; only avoiding the call itself is worth seconds.

## VERIFIED: the guest `toString()` render is 3.2s over 3,400,000 calls

The assumption that the non-combo path's ~3 us is the guest render was NOT measured until now, and
measuring it changed the scale:

```
[TOSTR] 3,400,000 renders, 3.238s, 952 ns avg
```

**3.4M renders, not the 800,000 map-key derivations** — the render recurses through nested values,
so it is called several times per derivation. At 952 ns each that is **3.2s of a ~80s boot (~4%)**,
the largest single quantity this goal has found, and it sits under `key_str_mut_in`.

### The admission rule that makes a memo provable rather than hopeful

A memo here cannot change the answer — same function, fewer calls — so the whole question is
invalidation. `stringify_memo` already exists but is CALL-SCOPED (it lives only while one outer
`String.valueOf` is active) and requires the VM's transitive effect proof to accept the concrete
`toString` as pure. Purity of the METHOD is not immutability of the OBJECT, so extending the
lifetime naively would be a silent wrong-answer bug.

The provable rule: **a class whose instance fields are ALL `final` cannot change after
construction**, and that is readable straight from the class file (`ACC_FINAL` on every non-static
field). Combined with the existing purity proof, a render of such an object is stable for the
object's lifetime. `Direction`, `Identifier`, `ResourceKey$InternKey` and `BlockState` — the four
classes the key census ranked — are exactly that shape.

Remaining hole to close deliberately, not by omission: reflective writes (`reflect.rs` can set a
field regardless of `final`). Those are rare and can bump a global memo epoch, which is cheap
because it costs nothing on the common path.

⚠ Not built yet. The measured prize is ~3.2s; the previous two changes in this funnel measured
0.08s and 0s, so this one gets a hit-rate counter AND the bit-exact gates before any claim.

### ⚠ A default `-Seq` that clusters one arm: `off,on,on,off,off,on`

The render-memo A/B ran the harness default sequence and produced this:

```
run cfg  done_s  wall_s
1   off  33.527   94.8
2   on   32.711  114.2
3   on   30.933  114.6
4   off  29.287   87.6
5   off  28.450   84.3
```

The per-arm means favour `off` (memo ENABLED) by ~1.4s on Done — and that is not a result. Both
`on` runs landed in the same slow window (wall 114s against 84-95s), because the default sequence
puts runs 2 and 3 adjacent in the same arm while the box was busy. The wall column shows the
machine quieting monotonically across the batch, so an arm's mean here is mostly a function of WHEN
its runs happened.

This is the same failure the two-binary harness was fixed for, and the flag harness inherits it
from its `-Seq` default rather than from its logic. `A,B,B,A,A,B` is balanced in COUNT but not in
POSITION: it gives one arm two adjacent slots in the middle of the batch.

⇒ Read the PAIRED deltas (added to `boot_flag_ab.ps1` earlier this session), not the arm means, and
prefer a strictly alternating `-Seq` when the box is drifting. A count-balanced sequence is not a
drift-balanced one.

## RESULT: the render memo is worth ~1.2s on Done, and NOTHING resolvable on wall

Paired A/B through `RAVA_NO_KEYRENDER_MEMO` (`on` = memo DISABLED), six boots:

```
run cfg  done_s  wall_s          off = memo ENABLED
1   off  33.527   94.8
2   on   32.711  114.2
3   on   30.933  114.6
4   off  29.287   87.6
5   off  28.450   84.3   <- the cleanest pair in the batch:
6   on   29.692   84.4   <- adjacent runs, wall within 0.1s
```

Two independent reads agree:

* **the cleanest pair** (runs 5/6, same machine to within 0.1s of wall): Done **−1.242s** with the
  memo;
* **min-of-N on Done**: 28.450 vs 29.692 = **−1.242s**, the same number.

Against a prediction of ~0.9s registered BEFORE the run. Mechanism verified independently: 99.7%
hit rate over admitted objects, gates bit-exact.

### ⛔ But the goal is WALL, and on wall this is not measurable

`min-of-N` wall: **84.3 vs 84.4 — 0.1s, i.e. nothing.** The same batch spans 84.3 to 114.6 seconds
of wall for the SAME binary, so this box's wall noise is tens of seconds and a 1.2s effect is far
below its resolution.

That is the honest reading, and it is a statement about the measurement as much as the change:

★ **A 1-second lever cannot be demonstrated on wall on this machine.** Every lever this goal has
found is between 0.08s and 1.2s. Proving any of them "rock-solid" against wall requires either an
effect an order of magnitude larger, or a wall measurement whose spread is under a second — and
this batch shows the spread is ~30s.

⇒ Done is the only metric here with enough resolution to see this class of change, and Done says
the memo works. Kept default-ON: bit-exact, mechanism-verified, −1.2s on the metric that can see
it, with a kill switch.

## Cross-call `toString` persistence — removal REJECTED (2026-07-31)

The call-scoped stringify memo remains useful; this decision concerns only the
new layer that retained renders after the outer `String.valueOf` returned.
The generic `RAVA_PERSIST_STAT` census reached exactly 500,000 outcomes on a
fresh canonical run: 102,288 call-scoped hits, **343 cross-call hits**, 378,730
misses, 16,859 stores and 1,780 non-admissions. Cross-call hits were therefore
0.069% of all observed outcomes while every cross-call miss paid an epoch check
and a TLS hash-table lookup.

To isolate the layer, a temporary generic `RAVA_NO_STRINGIFY_PERSIST` switch
left the call-scoped memo enabled. `bench/canonical_run.ps1` used six fresh
P-core processes in strict alternating order; every run produced
`8790f04ace726ecf`:

| Run | Persistence | Setup ms | Fill ms | Total ms |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | on | 34059 | 6919 | 40978 |
| 2 | off | 32386 | 7114 | 39500 |
| 3 | on | 32045 | 6864 | 38909 |
| 4 | off | 31937 | 7154 | 39091 |
| 5 | on | 32588 | 7012 | 39600 |
| 6 | off | 34028 | 7271 | 41299 |

Median total was 39,600 ms with persistence and 39,500 ms without it; paired
deltas change sign (off minus on: +1478, -182, -1699 ms). That is insufficient
evidence of a speed win, but it is also not permission to remove a heap-path
mechanism without the required GC gate.

The attempted removal of persistence, its reflective-write invalidation and
the temporary switch crashed the 2 MiB nursery stress run with Windows access
violation `0xC0000005` before emitting a hash. An isolated binary built from
the pre-removal commit `1a7dd1f` completed the identical command with
`SETUP_MS=78895`, `FILL_MS=14588` and hash `8790f04ace726ecf`. Therefore the
removal is **REJECTED for correctness**, not accepted as an optimization. Keep
the existing cross-call cache and its invalidation contract; it needs a
root-cause fix or a broader GC-stability proof before its performance value can
be reconsidered.

## Fresh serial PC-stack revalidation (2026-08-03)

This is diagnostic evidence only. `release-diag` was rebuilt with
`next-gen-gc,wall-profile`, then `bench/pcstack_boot.ps1` ran one ordinary
`server.jar` boot on P-cores with all restore/checkpoint/stackful controls
cleared. It reached `Starting minecraft server version` in 62.5 s; the guest
log placed `Environment:` at 38 s and the marker at 61 s. This run is not a
production timing result and does not change the open `wall < 20 s`, `Done <
10 s` gate.

The four 10 s PC-sampled coordinator blocks remained broad rather than
revealing a new goal-sized leaf:

| diagnostic block | leading JIT self-time | leading bridge attribution | conclusion |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12.7 s | `WallBlock.lambda$makeShapes$0` 40.7%; compile 21.4% | `StateHolder -> Map.get` 44.0%; `Reference2ObjectArrayMap -> reference2ObjectEntrySet` 22.3% | registry/block-state construction |
| 26.1 s | `BlockStateBase.initCache` 51.5%; compile 14.4% | the same `Map.get` site 31.1%; entry-set 15.6% | block-state cache construction |
| 40.0 s | `BlockStateBase.initCache` 58.8%; compile 20.2% | the same sites fall to 24.0% and 12.0% | shape/cache work plus compilation |
| 55.4 s | compile 23.6%; `MapDecoder.compressedDecode` 22.8% | input, list, sort, and codec calls spread across 188 sites | datapack/codec and registry work |

Across those samples, the recurrent host leaves were `Heap::gc`, allocator
paths, `memchr`, `Vm::jit_call_body`, `invokevirtual`, `jit_direct_probe`, and
native owner dispatch. None is independently large enough to turn a roughly
60 s pre-world boot into the required sub-20 s wall. This agrees with ETW:
the limiting work is generic coordinator guest invoke/dispatch/GC execution,
not an idle ring worker or a single Map/iterator cache.

The next admissible tracer bullet is therefore a function-level measurement of
the generic invoke and GC ownership boundary. It must not key behavior on a
jar, class, method name, hash, elapsed time, prior result, snapshot, or
checkpoint. A worker-only direct-call change has already been priced below the
wall target because this serial window precedes the ring phase.

fork shapes. A diagnostic pass using the existing iterator matcher found only

| `BlockState.initCache()V` | 14,751 | 1,296 | 500 | no | object loop, not fork-safe |

The scan emitted no sound high-ROI target. This is not a jar-specific rejection:
the gate is the generic transitive compiled/allocation/fork-safety proof, and
unknown or unsafe callees remain on the serial path. In the same diagnostic
window the wall sampler measured 38.2% JIT execution, 26.4% native bridges, and
20.4% JIT callback dispatch; `initCache` was 45.3% of JIT self-time while
Cranelift compilation was 18.6% of that block. Therefore widening the current
iterator matcher or adding a direct loop shortcut cannot deliver the required
wall reduction without first closing the generic worker-safe invoke/GC boundary.

Verdict: iterator/numeric lowering is rejected as a bounded next step. Keep the
probe and target census diagnostic-only; no production routing or no-adapt
admission change was made.

| 630 | ❌ **THE IMPLICIT-NULL-TRAP SHORTCUT IS WITHDRAWN: JIT `Ref` VALUES INDEX `ObjDesc`, AND LINUX HAS NO TRAP-TO-NPE PATH** | 2026-09-24. A scout proposed deleting one explicit JIT null branch based on HotSpot's implicit SIGSEGV trap; source verification disproved the premise. `fields_prim.rs::native_getfield_handle` masks the operand to low 32 bits and indexes `ObjDesc` at `ctx_cell+16 + handle*16` — it does not dereference a guest-object pointer. Null (`0`) and the first live handle both index slot 0, because `Heap::put_object` allocates the first handle as `objects.len() == 0`; deleting the branch can return the first object's field instead of throwing NPE. The existing empty `FieldBlob` sentinel protects dead handles, not handle 0. Workspace search found no Linux `sigaction`/SIGSEGV JIT deopt handler; `crash_handler.rs` is Windows-only diagnostics. Thus the proposed 2-3 instruction removal is UNSOUND and not an implementable local speed lever. Do not remove the guards. A correct fault-based path would require a separate signal-to-JIT-PC/NPE design and cannot be justified as a bounded optimization.
